chapter_theme: Energy of mind is the only possession that truly belongs to a person. Wealth leaves and returns, but this inner drive sets how high one rises, and without it strength and even humanity count for little.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: energy outranks the wealth it causes (591-594), the rise of those who have it (595-597), and the low standing of those who lack it (598-600).

591.reading: What makes someone 'one who has' is energy of mind; without it, do people really have even what they have?
591.nuance: Ownership is put in question, not merely wealth's worth. Parimelazhagar supplies a practical reason: without the power to guard it, they will lose it too.

592.reading: Possession of the inner drive is real possession; possession of goods does not stay and slips away.
592.nuance: The verse's word is உள்ளம், not ஊக்கம். Parimelazhagar makes the identification by metonymy, and Pope's '(energy of)' imports it, so the verse itself may be claiming somewhat more broadly that the mind is the true holding.

593.reading: Those who hold steady energy as their cash in hand do not fret, 'We have lost our gains'.
593.nuance: கைத்து is money in the hand, and the image is the verse's point: energy is liquid in a way that lost property is not. Their calm is a calculation of assets, not detachment, and this differs from the equanimity grounded in fate at 379.

594.reading: Prosperity itself asks the way and goes to the one whose energy does not waver.
594.nuance: Wealth is personified as a traveller who asks directions, so the seeker has become the sought. Parimelazhagar glosses அசைவின்மை as not flagging in hardship.

595.reading: The length of a water-flower's stem matches the depth of the water, and a person's height matches their inner drive.
595.nuance: Parimelazhagar notes the point of the image: the stem keeps lengthening as long as the water rises, so there is no fixed ceiling. The analogy has a gap, though: water is outside the plant, whereas the mind is within. 'Lotus' is Pope's and Kalaignar's addition; the verse says only மலர்.

positions.position: The height gained is worldly: increase in wealth and military force.
What is measured by the mind is energy itself, so the verse says how energy arises.

596.reading: Whatever you think about, think of rising; even if it is thrust aside, it has the quality of not having been thrust aside.
596.nuance: The verse names nothing that thrusts the aim aside. 'Fate' comes from Pope and from Parimelazhagar's பால்வகை, so this is less clearly a verse about fate than it appears in English.

positions.position: Even if fate denies kings the height, the aim stands: good people will not blame it, since their exertion did not fail.
positions.quote: அவ்வுயர்ச்சி பால்வகையாற் கூடிற்றில்லையாயினும், அக்கருத்துத் தள்ளாமை நீர்மையுடைத்து.

positions.position: A failed high aim is equal to having achieved it, and is beyond blame.
This is an instruction: even if it does not succeed, do not give up the thought.

597.reading: The strong in mind do not give way when things fall apart, as a bull elephant holds its ground under a sheaf of arrows.
597.nuance: Parimelazhagar reads a crossover: 'not giving way' belongs to the elephant and 'upholding one's greatness' to the strong, so that each half lends the other its verb.

598.reading: Those without inner drive never reach, in this world, the proud joy of saying 'we have been generous'.
598.nuance: செருக்கு is a fault in 431, yet here it is a joy worth wanting. Generosity is presented as something one may feel proud about, and this is not a usual picture of selfless giving.

positions.position: உள்ளம் is energy: without it the chain of effort, wealth, giving and pride never starts.
positions.quote: ஊக்கம் இல்லையாகவே முயற்சி, பொருள், கொடை செருக்கு இவை முறையே இலவாம்

positions.position: உள்ளம் is the eagerness to give: without it one can't take pride in being a giver.

599.reading: Though its body is huge and its tusks are sharp, an elephant fears when a tiger attacks.
599.nuance: The verse says nothing about energy or kings. Parimelazhagar names it an allegory (பிறிது மொழிதல்), and the chapter's setting is all that justifies the moral.

600.reading: A person's real firmness is the abundance of the inner drive; those without it are trees, and being human is the only difference.
600.nuance: Parimelazhagar sharpens the insult: trees bear fruit and serve in temples, houses, chariots and ships, so the only thing left separating such people from trees is that they are not as useful. He also reads உரம் as understanding, as in 24, which joins will and intelligence.

links.note: Both turn on the same word. In 594 wealth seeks out அசைவிலா energy. In 371 அசைவின்மை is itself produced by a fate of gain. The causal arrow reverses, so the question becomes whether steadfastness is one's own at all.

The elephant carries opposite morals three verses apart: under arrows it models unbreakable resolve, and before a tiger it is bulk without resolve. Parimelazhagar accepts this by locating the difference in the tiger's energy.

Both speak of the pride of giving (செருக்கு) and both root it in exertion. 613 names the vocabulary of labour and liberality that 598 only implies, so generosity is shown to have an economic foundation.

The Kural keeps naming the one true wealth: learning in 400, what is heard in 411, grace in 241, and energy here. Each dismisses ordinary wealth, but they cannot all be the sole true possession. Each is best read as a chapter's rhetorical peak.

Tree-people appear for two different lacks: kindly regard in 576 and energy in 600, and again for human quality in 997. The tree image stands for whatever a chapter takes to be essential to being human.

source_issues: 591: Manakkudavar's text reads ஒற்றரையுடைமை, which makes no sense here and may be a garbled word.
593: The verse's first word is missing its first letter (க்கம் for ஆக்கம்), as the commentaries show. Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned.
594: The verse's first word is missing its first letter (க்கம் for ஆக்கம்), as the commentaries show.
598: Parimelazhagar's text reads பெற்றார் where the sense and the verse's எய்தார் need a negative such as பெறார்.
599: The verse's second line has a corrupted character at the start (஦வ்ருஉம்); the commentary gives வெரூஉம். Parimelazhagar's lemma reads பரியத for பரியது.
